misconceptions.claim: All the molecules of a gas at a given temperature move with the same speed.
misconceptions.why: Molecular speeds are distributed over a wide range (the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution); only the mean translational kinetic energy is fixed by the temperature. Collisions constantly redistribute energy between molecules.
misconceptions.correction: T fixes the average: (1/2) m <v^2> = (3/2) k T. Individual molecules move at very different speeds, from near zero to many times the root mean square speed, and the temperature of the gas is a statistical statement about the ensemble.

misconceptions.claim: The pressure of a gas is caused by the molecules pushing on the walls.
misconceptions.why: That is a good picture, but it is incomplete: the pressure is the rate of momentum transfer at the wall, and the molecules are not constantly pushing - they are in free flight between collisions.
misconceptions.correction: Each collision transfers 2 m v_x of momentum to the wall (in the wall's frame the molecule's normal momentum reverses). Summing over all molecules gives P = (1/3) (N/V) m <v^2>, which is the kinetic-theory result: pressure is a consequence of molecular motion, not of a steady push.

misconceptions.claim: The molar heat capacity of a gas is the same whether it is heated at constant pressure or at constant volume.
misconceptions.why: At constant pressure the gas expands and does work, so more heat is needed for the same temperature rise. The two heat capacities differ by exactly R.
misconceptions.correction: C_P - C_V = R for an ideal gas. For a monatomic gas C_V = 3R/2 and C_P = 5R/2; for a diatomic gas at ordinary temperatures C_V = 5R/2 and C_P = 7R/2, the extra degree of freedom being rotation.

workbook.question: A 2.0 litre container holds nitrogen gas at 300 K and 1.00 atm. Find the number of moles, the number of molecules, and the root mean square speed of the molecules. Take R = 8.314 J/(mol K) and the mass of N2 as 28 x 1.66 x 10^-27 kg.
Starting from the elastic collisions of molecules with the walls of a container, derive the kinetic-theory expression P = (1/3) (N/V) m v_rms^2 for the pressure of an ideal gas.
workbook.answer: Consider a molecule of mass m with velocity components (v_x, v_y, v_z) in a cube of side L. A collision with a wall reverses v_x, so the impulse delivered to the wall is 2 m v_x. If the molecule makes n_x collisions per second with that wall, the force on it is 2 m v_x n_x, and since it crosses the cube n_x = v_x / (2L) times per second, the force is m v_x^2 / L. Summing over all molecules and over the three directions, the total force on the wall is (m/L) sum(v_x^2 + v_y^2 + v_z^2) = (m/L) N <v^2> for a gas in equilibrium. Dividing by the wall area A = L^2 gives P = (m N <v^2>) / (V L) = (N/V) m <v^2> / 3, since <v^2> = <v_x^2> + <v_y^2> + <v_z^2> = 3 <v_x^2> by isotropy. Hence P = (1/3) (N/V) m v_rms^2.

workbook.question: A gas is compressed in a cylinder with a piston, and the temperature stays constant. Explain what happens to the rms speed, to the pressure, and to the time between successive collisions of a given molecule with the container wall.
workbook.answer: At constant temperature (1/2) m v_rms^2 = (3/2) k T is unchanged, so the rms speed does not change - compression at constant temperature changes only how the molecules are packed, not how fast they move. The pressure rises, because P = (1/3) (N/V) m v_rms^2 and N/V increases as the volume falls: halving the volume doubles the pressure. The time between successive collisions of a given molecule with the wall falls, because the wall is closer to the molecule on average, and there are correspondingly more molecules per unit volume, so the collision rate goes up roughly as 1/sqrt(V). This is why a gas heats up when it is compressed rapidly: there is no time for the heat to escape, and the work done on the gas becomes internal energy.

units.summary: Curved mirrors turn the law of reflection into an imaging device. Everything in the unit rests on one approximation - rays close to the principal axis - and on one convention that, used inconsistently, produces most of the wrong answers.
facts: The focal length of a spherical mirror is half the radius of curvature, f = R/2; concave mirrors converge and convex mirrors diverge.
A convex mirror always produces a virtual, upright and diminished image of a real object, which is why it is the safe choice for a vehicle mirror.
The mirror equation 1/f = 1/v + 1/u and the magnification m = -v/u hold under the New Cartesian sign convention.

Three principal rays suffice for any ray diagram: parallel to the axis (reflected through the focus), through the centre of curvature (reflected back on itself), and through the focus (reflected parallel to the axis).
The point focus of a spherical mirror exists only in the paraxial approximation; spherical aberration grows rapidly with the aperture.
The 18 hexagonal segments of the JWST mirror are aligned to act as a single 6.5 m primary, focused to a precision of a small fraction of the width of a human hair.
A spherical mirror has a single focus only while the aperture is small compared with the radius of curvature; beyond that, spherical aberration spreads the focus and the image softens with age.
conditions: Mirror and lens formulae are paraxial: the rays must be close to the principal axis. Wide apertures require real ray tracing or an aspherical surface such as a parabola.
A real image can be caught on a screen; a virtual image cannot be projected, which is the physical difference behind the two categories.
Mixing sign conventions is the single most common source of wrong signs; fix one convention and use it in every diagram.
For a mirror moving at speed, the image can appear to move faster than light; no information travels faster than light because the image is an optical construction, not a material object.
The mirror equation and magnification are paraxial results; a wide field of view needs aberration-corrected designs such as the Ritchey-Chretien and active mirrors like JWST's.

mysteries.question: Can an optical system form a perfect image of an extended object across a wide field of view?
mysteries.note: Aberration theory rules out perfect imaging with simple surfaces; multi-element and wave-optics designs trade cost against the remaining errors, and no system is perfect.

mysteries.question: How far can real-time adaptive optics push atmospheric correction for ground-based telescopes?
mysteries.note: Correction works extremely well for well-resolved guide stars, and the limit is set by sensor speed, guide-star availability and photon flux.

misconceptions.claim: A convex mirror always forms a virtual, upright and diminished image, whatever the position of the object.
misconceptions.why: This is true, but students often reach for it as a slogan rather than as a consequence, and then cannot explain the special case of an object at infinity, where the image tends to a point at the focus.
misconceptions.correction: A convex mirror always has a virtual focus behind the mirror, so the image lies behind the mirror at a distance less than f for any real object. The image is upright, diminished (0 < |m| < 1) and lies between the pole and the focus. As the object moves to infinity the image approaches the focus and its size tends to zero.

misconceptions.claim: The image in a concave mirror is always real.
misconceptions.why: A concave mirror forms a real image only when the object lies outside the centre of curvature. Between the focus and the mirror the image is virtual, upright and magnified - the face in a shaving mirror is exactly this case.
misconceptions.correction: For a concave mirror with f = R/2: object beyond C gives a real, inverted, diminished image between C and F; object at C gives the image at C; object between C and F gives a real, inverted, magnified image beyond C; object at F gives the image at infinity; object between F and the pole gives a virtual, upright, magnified image behind the mirror.

misconceptions.claim: The mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f is true for any spherical mirror and any position of the object.
misconceptions.why: The formula is a paraxial result: it holds for rays close to the principal axis and for small apertures. A spherical mirror with a wide aperture has a different focus for different zones of the surface - spherical aberration - and the simple formula no longer describes the image.
misconceptions.correction: The mirror formula is exact within the paraxial (Gaussian) approximation. It requires the object and image to be small compared with the radius of curvature and the rays to make small angles with the axis. Parabolic mirrors are used for large apertures because a parabola focuses exactly, at the price of the off-axis aberrations that a sphere also has.

workbook.question: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find the position, nature and size of the image (use the Cartesian sign convention: u = -30 cm, f = -10 cm).
workbook.answer: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f gives 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = -1/10 + 1/30 = (-3 + 1)/30 = -2/30, so v = -15 cm. The image is 15 cm in front of the mirror, between F (10 cm) and C (20 cm), so it is real and inverted. Magnification m = -v/u = -(-15)/(-30) = -0.5, so the image is half the size of the object.

workbook.question: Derive the mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f for a spherical mirror from the paraxial geometry of a ray parallel to the principal axis.
workbook.answer: Take the pole as origin, the principal axis as the x-axis, and let C be the centre of curvature at distance R, so F is at R/2. A ray from the top of an object of height h strikes the mirror at P and is reflected through F. For small angles, a spherical mirror approximates a parabola, so the incident and reflected rays make equal angles with the normal at P. Using the small-angle geometry of the triangles formed with the axis, the ray geometry gives the relation h/h' = (R - v)/v, where h' is the image height. Combining this with the similar triangles for the ray through C, which gives h/h' = v/u, one finds h'/h = -v/u (the minus sign recording the inversion for a real image). Eliminating h/h' between the two relations and using f = R/2 gives 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. The derivation assumes paraxial rays throughout.

workbook.question: Why is a convex mirror fitted as the rear-view mirror in a vehicle, while a concave mirror is not, even though the convex mirror makes objects look smaller?
workbook.answer: The deciding property is the field of view and the nature of the image. A convex mirror always forms a virtual, upright, diminished image for every object position, so the driver sees a wide field behind the vehicle at once, and the image is upright so that left and right are not reversed. A concave mirror would form a real, inverted image for objects beyond the centre of curvature, which is both disorienting and dangerous, and for close objects it would give a magnified real image with no useful field. The convex mirror therefore trades resolution for safety, and a flat mirror is used inside the car precisely because it preserves size and does not distort distances.

units.summary: Refraction at a plane boundary is Snell's law, but the interesting physics is in the consequences: the lateral shift through a slab, the shallower apparent depth of a pool, and total internal reflection, which is the whole basis of fibre optics.
facts: Snell's law reads n1 sin(theta1) = n2 sin(theta2), with n = c/v the refractive index; the frequency of light is unchanged at the boundary while its speed and wavelength change.
A plane-parallel slab displaces the emergent ray sideways while keeping it parallel to the incident ray; the displacement grows with thickness and with obliquity.
Total internal reflection requires n1 > n2 and an incidence angle above the critical angle theta_c = arcsin(n2/n1), about 41.1 degrees for crown glass (n = 1.52) against air.
Viewed near-normally, an object in water appears shallower by a factor of about n, so a 1.5 m depth reads as about 1.1 m.
Optical fibres work by repeated total internal reflection; the acceptance angle is fixed by the numerical aperture of the core and cladding.
In the wave picture refraction follows from phase continuity at the boundary: the phase must match across it, which is Snell's law in a different costume.
Snell's law is a statement about phase continuity across a boundary: the change of direction is what keeps the wavefronts in step, and the same law governs light as a wave and as a quantum field.
conditions: Snell's law assumes an isotropic, homogeneous, stationary, non-absorbing medium and a smooth interface; rough or moving boundaries change the result.
Near the critical angle the transmitted ray grazes the surface and the reflection coefficient approaches one.
The simple apparent-depth rule (divide by n) holds only for near-normal viewing; at oblique angles the correct factor is cos(theta')/cos(theta).
Dispersion - the wavelength dependence of n - is neglected in the basic model but must be included whenever white light is involved.
Fermat's principle fixes the path of least time rather than least distance, and that distinction is why a refracted ray bends towards the normal in a denser medium.

mysteries.question: Can an image be formed that is not limited by the diffraction limit?
mysteries.note: Superlenses using negative-index materials beat the diffraction limit at a single frequency; extending the idea to a usable bandwidth remains an open and difficult problem.

mysteries.question: Why does light slow down in a medium without losing energy?
mysteries.note: The classical account through the material's dielectric response is standard, while the fully microscopic picture of coherent forward scattering is subtler.

Explain why a swimming pool looks shallower at the far end, and derive the apparent depth for oblique viewing.

misconceptions.claim: Light slows down in glass and keeps that slower speed when it comes back into air, so the emerging ray is displaced but otherwise unchanged.
misconceptions.why: Speed is a property of the wave in the medium, and the medium it is in determines it. On returning to air the speed returns to c; what survives is the direction set by Snell's law.
misconceptions.correction: The speed is c/n in the medium, so it returns to c on leaving the glass. Snell's law n1 sin(theta1) = n2 sin(theta2) is satisfied at each boundary, and because the two faces of a parallel slab are parallel the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray, displaced sideways by t sin(i - r)/cos r.

misconceptions.claim: Total internal reflection happens when the angle of incidence is large enough, whatever the two media.
misconceptions.why: It requires the ray to travel from the optically denser medium to the optically rarer one. Going the other way (air into glass) the ray always emerges, because the refracted angle can never exceed 90 degrees.
misconceptions.correction: TIR needs n1 > n2 and theta1 greater than the critical angle, sin(theta_c) = n2/n1. For glass to air the critical angle is about 41.8 degrees (n = 1.5), and for water to air about 48.6 degrees (n = 1.333).

misconceptions.claim: A coin at the bottom of a bowl of water appears at its true depth, because light travels in straight lines.
misconceptions.why: Light travels in straight lines in each medium, but the refraction at the surface bends the ray towards the normal, so the eye traces the ray back in a straight line and gets the wrong origin.
misconceptions.correction: For near-normal viewing the apparent depth is h' = h (n2/n1) = h / n for an object in water viewed from air. A 10 cm deep pool therefore looks about 7.5 cm deep with n = 1.333.

workbook.question: A ray of light in water (n = 1.333) meets the water-air surface at an angle of incidence of 40 degrees. Find the angle of refraction in air, and state whether total internal reflection would occur at this incidence.
workbook.answer: Snell's law: 1.333 sin 40 degrees = 1 x sin(theta2), so sin(theta2) = 1.333 x 0.6428 = 0.8569 and theta2 = 58.9 degrees (about 59 degrees). The critical angle for water to air satisfies sin(theta_c) = 1/1.333 = 0.7502, so theta_c = 48.6 degrees. Since 40 degrees < 48.6 degrees, the ray is well below the critical angle and no total internal reflection occurs.

workbook.question: Derive the expression for the lateral shift d produced when a ray passes through a plane-parallel slab of thickness t and refractive index n, with angle of incidence i and angle of refraction r.
workbook.answer: Inside the slab the ray travels along a path inclined at r to the normal, so over the thickness t it moves laterally by t tan r. If the emergent ray were continued straight it would travel from the point of incidence at angle i and would be displaced by t tan i. The lateral shift is the difference between these two offsets measured at the exit plane. The perpendicular distance between the incident and emergent rays is d cos r, and the geometry gives d cos r = t tan i - t tan r, so d = t (tan i - tan r) / cos r. Using Snell's law, sin i = n sin r, this can be written d = t sin(i - r) / cos r, which vanishes when i = r (normal incidence).

workbook.question: Explain why an optical fibre guides light, and deduce the condition on the angle of entry for a glass core of index 1.5 surrounded by cladding of index 1.4.
workbook.answer: Light entering the core strikes the core-cladding boundary from inside the optically denser medium. If the angle of incidence at that boundary exceeds the critical angle, sin(theta_c) = n_clad/n_core = 1.4/1.5 = 0.9333, so theta_c = 68.9 degrees, the ray is totally internally reflected and is guided along the fibre with no energy lost out of the core. In practice the light bounces many times per millimetre, so even a small loss per bounce is negligible. The acceptance condition in terms of the angle theta of the entering ray to the fibre axis is sin(theta) <= sqrt(n_core^2 - n_clad^2) = sqrt(2.25 - 1.96) = sqrt(0.29) = 0.539, so theta <= 32.6 degrees; this number is the numerical aperture of the fibre, and it sets how much light can be coupled in.

units.summary: A prism is a device that separates wavelengths as it bends them. The unit connects geometry to spectroscopy: the apex angle sets the deviation, the refractive index sets the dispersion, and the spectrum is the primary chemical and astronomical fingerprint of light.
facts: A prism deviates light because its faces are not parallel, and it disperses light because the refractive index depends on wavelength - normally n is larger for blue than for red.
For a thin prism of small apex angle A, the deviation is approximately d = (n - 1) A.
The dispersive power w = (n_v - n_r)/(n_y - 1) is nearly constant for a given material, which is why glasses can be sorted into crown and flint families.
Minimum deviation occurs when the ray path is symmetric (i = e), giving n = sin((A + d_m)/2) / sin(A/2) - the standard laboratory method.
A hollow prism filled with a liquid measures that liquid's refractive index by the same minimum-deviation method.
The rainbow is refraction plus one internal reflection plus dispersion in water droplets, which is why the primary bow has an angle of about 42 degrees.

At minimum deviation the ray path is symmetric, so the refractive index can be measured without knowing the prism's apex angle precisely - which is why the spectrometer method is the reference technique.
conditions: The thin-prism approximation requires a small apex angle; thick prisms need the exact two-surface treatment with Snell's law applied twice.
Dispersion is small - the index changes by only about 0.01 to 0.02 across the visible for glass - so a single prism gives a spectrum whose orders overlap and may need a second prism to isolate.
Deviation depends on the refractive index of the surrounding medium: a prism in water disperses far less than the same prism in air.
Refractive index depends on temperature as well as wavelength, so precision spectroscopy requires controlling the temperature of the prism.
The small-angle formula n = 1 + A/2D is an approximation that fails beyond about 10 degrees of deviation; real work uses the exact minimum-deviation relation.

mysteries.question: How do modern observatories push spectroscopy to fainter objects than the classical prism or grating allowed?
mysteries.note: Very large telescopes, échelle spectrographs and interferometry have extended the reach, and each gain is limited by photon collection and detector noise.

mysteries.question: Can a dispersive element be built that disperses without deviating, or deviates without dispersing?
mysteries.note: Compound and metamaterial designs approach these limits, but causality constrains how well an achromatic, deviation-free element can behave over a finite bandwidth.

prompts: Given the deviation angles of red and violet light through a 60 degree prism, find the two refractive indices and hence the dispersive power.
Measure the angle of minimum deviation for a triangular glass prism, compute n, and repeat with a hollow prism filled with water.
Explain geometrically why the deviation of a prism does not grow in proportion to the thickness of the glass.
syllabusTopics: Relation between the angle of prism, minimum deviation and refractive index

misconceptions.claim: A prism deviates light because it slows the light down.
misconceptions.why: Slowing alone is not a deviation: the ray would resume its original direction on leaving, and a parallel-sided slab does exactly that. What bends the ray is the change of direction at each face, because the faces are not parallel.
misconceptions.correction: At the first face the ray bends towards the normal (r < i) and at the second face, where it goes from dense to rare, it bends away from the normal. Because the two faces are inclined at the apex angle A, the outgoing ray is displaced by the deviation delta, and for a thin prism delta = (n - 1) A.

misconceptions.claim: The angle of deviation of a prism is fixed, whatever the angle of incidence.
misconceptions.why: The deviation varies with incidence, and it has a minimum value when the path through the prism is symmetric. Using the deviation for an arbitrary incidence is the source of most errors.
misconceptions.correction: The deviation is a function of i and e, with i + e = A + delta. It is smallest for i = e, the symmetric path, and that minimum is the one tabulated. At minimum deviation n = sin((A + delta_m)/2) / sin(A/2).

misconceptions.claim: The dispersive power of a glass is the difference between its refractive indices for violet and red light.
misconceptions.why: That difference is a useful measure of dispersion but it is not the dimensionless dispersive power, which is normalised so that glasses can be compared fairly.
misconceptions.correction: omega = (n_v - n_r) / (n_y - 1). For a crown glass with n_v = 1.530, n_r = 1.514 and n_y = 1.517, the difference n_v - n_r = 0.016 while the dispersive power is 0.016 / 0.517 = 0.031.

workbook.question: A prism of apex angle 60 degrees and refractive index 1.5 is used in the minimum-deviation position. Calculate the angle of minimum deviation, and verify the relation n = sin((A + delta_m)/2) / sin(A/2).
workbook.answer: n = sin((A + delta_m)/2) / sin(A/2) gives 1.5 = sin((60 + delta_m)/2) / sin 30 degrees = 2 sin((60 + delta_m)/2), so sin((60 + delta_m)/2) = 0.75. Hence (60 + delta_m)/2 = 48.6 degrees and delta_m = 37.2 degrees (about 37 degrees). Substitution back gives sin(48.6)/sin(30) = 0.750/0.500 = 1.50, confirming the relation.

workbook.question: Derive the approximate deviation of a thin prism, delta = (n - 1) A.
workbook.answer: For a thin prism the angle of incidence i and the angle of emergence e are both small, and the refracted angles inside are r1 and r2 with r1 + r2 = A. From Snell's law at the first face, sin i = n sin r1, and since the angles are small, i = n r1. Similarly e = n r2. The total deviation is delta = (i - r1) + (e - r2) = (n - 1)(r1 + r2) = (n - 1) A. The result is independent of the angle of incidence, which is why a thin prism can be used as a spectrometer element: a thicker prism is dispersive but also strongly deviating.

workbook.question: A hollow prism with two parallel faces at 60 degrees is filled with water and used in the minimum-deviation position. Explain why the same instrument can measure the refractive index of a liquid, and state what the measurement gives.
workbook.answer: The hollow prism is an optical cell whose interior can be filled with any liquid; the glass walls only serve to hold the liquid and to define the two refracting faces at the apex angle A. The light passes through the liquid exactly as it would through a solid prism of the same apex angle, so the measured minimum deviation satisfies n_liquid = sin((A + delta_m)/2) / sin(A/2). With A = 60 degrees and a measured delta_m of 44.8 degrees, n = sin(52.4)/sin(30) = 0.792/0.500 = 1.58... more precisely, using the standard value for water near 1.333 the expected deviation is 2 sin^-1(n sin 30) - 60 = 2 x 41.8 - 60 = 23.6 degrees, and the measured deviation gives the liquid's index directly. The method needs a narrow slit and a spectrometer, since the deviation must be measured precisely.

units.summary: Lenses bend light to make images, and the thin-lens equation is the workhorse of the entire unit. What separates school physics from optical engineering is the list of assumptions that equation hides: thinness, paraxial rays, and a single refractive index.
facts: The thin-lens equation is 1/f = 1/v - 1/u under the usual sign convention, and the lensmaker's equation gives 1/f = (n - 1)(1/R1 - 1/R2) for a lens in air.
The power of a lens is P = 1/f in dioptres; for a lens immersed in a medium of index n_m it becomes (n_l/n_m - 1)(1/R1 - 1/R2).
A converging lens is thicker at the centre and a diverging lens is thinner at the centre; for a real object a diverging lens always gives a virtual, upright, diminished image.
In contact, P = P1 + P2; separated by a distance d, the equivalent power is 1/F = 1/f1 + 1/f2 - d/(f1 f2).
The human eye is a roughly 17 mm lens with a focal length of about 2.3 cm; accommodation works by changing the lens curvature so the image always lands on the retina.
Magnification m = v/u, and a real image is inverted and can be projected on a screen.

A lens forms a real or virtual image depending on where the object sits relative to the focal length, and the thin-lens treatment hides the thick-lens corrections and aberrations that real objectives need.
conditions: The thin-lens equation requires a lens thin compared with its focal length and paraxial rays; real camera and telescope lenses are thick assemblies whose elements cancel aberrations.
Chromatic aberration means f depends on wavelength, so a single glass lens focuses blue and red at different distances; an achromatic doublet combines glasses of different dispersion to cancel it.
Spherical aberration grows with aperture, so stopping down a camera trades brightness for sharpness - until diffraction takes over.
Depth of field depends on aperture and focal length as well as on the sensor, so it is a property of the optical system, not of the camera body.
The lensmaker's equation assumes a thin lens in air; a thick or multi-element system is described by its principal planes and effective focal length instead.

mysteries.question: How do observatories image exoplanets that are thousands of light-years away and a few pixels across?
mysteries.note: Coronagraphs, adaptive optics and interferometry are combined to suppress starlight by many orders of magnitude, and each step adds its own noise.

mysteries.question: Is there a fundamental limit to how small an optical element can be before diffraction dominates?
mysteries.note: Abbe's limit sets the classical bound and super-resolution can cross it only in restricted ways; how far this can be pushed for imaging remains an active question.

Design an achromatic doublet from two glass types and explain the trade-off between focal length, spherical aberration and cost.
Explain why closing the aperture improves depth of field but introduces diffraction blur, and find the aperture that balances the two.

misconceptions.claim: A converging lens always forms a real image.
misconceptions.why: The position of the object decides the case. Inside the focal length the image is virtual, upright and magnified - the image in a magnifying glass, and the near point of a relaxed eye.
misconceptions.correction: For a converging lens: object beyond 2f gives a real, inverted, diminished image between f and 2f; at 2f the image is at 2f and the same size; between f and 2f the image is real, inverted and magnified beyond 2f; at f the image is at infinity; inside f the image is virtual, upright and magnified, on the same side as the object.

misconceptions.claim: A lens's power depends on the glass it is made of and on how fast light travels in it.
misconceptions.why: The power of a lens in air depends only on its focal length, and the focal length is fixed by the geometry and by the refractive index relative to the surroundings. Speed alone does not set the power.
misconceptions.correction: P = 1/f in dioptres, with f in metres. From the lens-maker's formula, 1/f = (n - 1)(1/R1 - 1/R2) in air, so the power is set by the relative refractive index n_medium and the curvatures. A lens of the same shape but made of a denser glass has a shorter focal length and a greater power.

misconceptions.claim: Two thin lenses in contact can be replaced by a single lens whose power is the sum of their powers.
misconceptions.why: That is true only for thin lenses in contact, where the separation is negligible compared with the focal lengths and the lenses can be treated as a single element.
misconceptions.correction: In contact, P = P1 + P2. Separated by a distance d, the equivalent power is P = P1 + P2 - d P1 P2, and the separation term is exactly why telephoto and zoom combinations are designed with the spacing as a variable.

workbook.question: A converging lens of focal length 20 cm forms a real image of an object placed 60 cm from the lens. Find the image distance and the magnification, and state the power of the lens.
workbook.answer: 1/v = 1/f + 1/u with u = 60 cm and f = 20 cm gives 1/v = 1/20 - 1/60 = (3 - 1)/60 = 2/60, so v = 30 cm. The image is real and inverted, 30 cm from the lens. Magnification m = v/u = 30/60 = 0.5, so the image is half the object's size. Power P = 1/f = 1/0.20 = 5 D.

workbook.question: Derive the lens-maker's formula for a thin lens in air, 1/f = (n - 1)(1/R1 - 1/R2), from the refraction at the two spherical surfaces.
workbook.answer: For the first surface, refraction in a spherical surface gives n2/v1 - n1/u = (n2 - n1)/R1 with n1 = 1 and n2 = n. For the second surface, n/v - n/v1 = (1 - n)/R2, and adding the two equations eliminates the intermediate distance v1: n/v - 1/u = (n - 1)(1/R1 - 1/R2). For a thin lens the object and image distances are measured from the same plane, so 1/v - 1/u = 1/f, which identifies the lens-maker's formula. The sign convention (Cartesian, with light travelling in the positive direction) decides the signs of R1 and R2: a surface convex to the incident light has R1 positive.

workbook.question: A photographer stops the lens down from f/2.8 to f/16 to increase depth of field. Explain what is gained and what is lost, and identify the physical limit that eventually stops the gain.
workbook.answer: Stopping down reduces the diameter of the beam admitted by the lens, and a narrower beam makes the range of object distances that map to an acceptable circle of confusion smaller, so the depth of field grows - the gain. The cost is less light: the exposure time must be lengthened by the square of the stop ratio (about 32x in area between f/2.8 and f/16) or the ISO raised, and at slow speeds the image picks up camera shake. There is also a hard limit: a point object is imaged not as a point but as an Airy diffraction pattern of angular radius 1.22 lambda / D, so as the aperture is reduced the diffraction blur grows and eventually overwhelms the gain from the smaller geometric circle of confusion. The optimum is around f/8 to f/11 for a full-frame camera.

units.summary: Dispersion is the wavelength dependence of refractive index. It explains rainbows and chromatic aberration, it is the reason a spectrum carries chemical information, and it contains one of the sharpest traps in optics: the difference between phase velocity and the speed that carries information.
facts: Dispersion means n depends on wavelength, so different colours bend by different amounts and a lens focuses them at different distances.
Cauchy's empirical form n = A + B/lambda^2 gives an approximate wavelength dependence in transparent regions.
Normal dispersion - n rising as lambda falls - is what produces the familiar spectrum order from red to violet.
Anomalous dispersion near an absorption band reverses the sign of dn/dlambda, and a dispersive prism can then select a single narrow band from white light.
The group velocity v_g = c/(n - lambda dn/dlambda) can exceed c or become negative in anomalously dispersive media without violating relativity, because the phase velocity carries no information.
A spectrum is a fingerprint: the blackbody shape gives temperature, the line positions give composition, and the Doppler shift gives motion.
Glass has a larger refractive index for blue light than for red, so short wavelengths are bent more and a prism sends violet towards the inside of the spectrum.
conditions: Cauchy's two-parameter fit is valid only for normal dispersion in transparent regions; it diverges near a resonance and cannot describe absorption at all.
Information travels at the group velocity, so superluminal phase velocity is a feature of the mathematics, not a violation of causality.
At a boundary between media the frequency of light does not change; what changes is the speed and hence the wavelength - a classic examination trap.
Spectral lines are broadened by temperature, pressure and Doppler motion, and that broadening sets the precision with which a line centre can be measured.
In a dispersive medium the group velocity differs from the phase velocity, so the speed of light in glass quoted as c/n is a phase speed and not the speed at which a pulse front travels.

mysteries.question: Can a dispersion profile be engineered that resolves wavelengths beyond the diffraction limit of the device itself?
mysteries.note: Metasurface and metamaterial designs are actively pursuing this; causality and usable bandwidth are the limiting constraints.

mysteries.question: How are atomic energy levels and their linewidths set, and how far can they be predicted from first principles?
mysteries.note: Spectroscopy is precise enough to test atomic theory at parts per billion, which keeps refining rather than contradicting it.

prompts: Using Cauchy's formula and a measured index at two wavelengths, predict the order in which colours emerge from a prism.
Explain why the same prism shows a much narrower spectrum when immersed in water.
Compare the resolving power of a prism and a diffraction grating for the same beam width, and identify which is better for faint astronomical sources.

misconceptions.claim: Dispersion means that different colours travel at different speeds, and therefore the colour we see is the colour of the light itself.
misconceptions.why: The second part is wrong: the colour we perceive is set by the frequency, which is unchanged when light enters a medium. Only the speed and wavelength change.
misconceptions.correction: When light enters a medium its frequency is fixed by the source, so v = c/n and the wavelength shortens: lambda_medium = lambda_vacuum / n. A prism does not change the frequency of any component, so the spectrum it produces still has the same colours as the source; the prism only separates the directions of the different frequencies.

misconceptions.claim: The dispersive power of a glass is the difference between its refractive indices for violet and red light.
misconceptions.why: That difference is a measure of how much the glass disperses, but it is not the dimensionless dispersive power, which is normalised so that different glasses can be compared.
misconceptions.correction: omega = (n_v - n_r) / (n_y - 1). With n_v = 1.530, n_r = 1.514, n_y = 1.517 the difference is 0.016 but the dispersive power is 0.016 / 0.517 = 0.031. The normalisation matters because glasses differ in their overall index as well as in their dispersion.

misconceptions.claim: The speed of light in a medium can be greater than c, which shows that Einstein is wrong.
misconceptions.why: The speed that can exceed c is the group velocity of a strongly dispersive pulse, and the group velocity is not the speed at which information or a single crest travels. No signal outruns c.
misconceptions.correction: v_g = c / (n - lambda dn/dlambda) can be negative or greater than c near an absorption band, but the phase velocity c/n and the velocity of the front of a pulse never exceed c, and causality is preserved. The group velocity is a property of a pulse in a strongly dispersive medium, not a transport speed for anything.

workbook.question: A crown glass has refractive indices n_v = 1.530, n_y = 1.517 and n_r = 1.514. Find its dispersive power, and find the angle of deviation of a 60 degree prism of this glass at minimum deviation for the yellow line.
workbook.answer: Dispersive power omega = (n_v - n_r)/(n_y - 1) = (1.530 - 1.514)/(1.517 - 1) = 0.016/0.517 = 0.0310. For the yellow line, n = sin((A + delta_m)/2)/sin(A/2) gives 1.517 = sin((60 + delta_m)/2)/0.5, so sin((60 + delta_m)/2) = 0.7585 and (60 + delta_m)/2 = 49.3 degrees, hence delta_m = 38.6 degrees. The angular dispersion between the violet and red lines is then (n_v - n_r) A = 0.016 x 60 degrees = 0.96 degrees, which matches the typical figure of about 1 degree for a 60 degree crown-glass prism.

workbook.question: Derive the angular dispersion produced by a thin prism between two wavelengths, and relate it to the dispersive power of the glass.
workbook.answer: For a thin prism the deviation for a wavelength lambda is delta = (n(lambda) - 1) A. The angular dispersion between two wavelengths is therefore delta_v - delta_r = (n_v - n_r) A. The dispersive power is defined as omega = (n_v - n_r)/(n_y - 1), so the angular dispersion can be written delta_v - delta_r = omega (n_y - 1) A, which shows that for a fixed glass and apex angle the dispersion is proportional to omega. Since the deviation of a prism is small, a prism is used as the dispersing element of a spectrometer and a telescope is used to view the spectrum without further deviation.

workbook.question: A spectroscope uses a collimator, a prism and a telescope. Explain the function of each part, and explain how the same arrangement can be used to measure the wavelength of a spectral line.
workbook.answer: The collimator is a lens with a narrow slit at its focal plane, so the light from the slit emerges as a parallel beam; without it the prism would simply produce a blurred image of the source. The prism disperses the beam by an amount that depends on wavelength, so the emergent beam contains a spectrum. The telescope then focuses that spectrum onto the eyepiece, and the scale on the prism table or the vernier measures the deviation angle for each colour. Because the deviation of a prism in the minimum-deviation position is known as a function of n, and n as a function of wavelength, measuring the deviation of an unknown line and inverting the relation yields its wavelength. This is how stellar spectra give the composition of stars and how the redshift of a galaxy is measured.

units.summary: Electric charge is the first conserved quantity a student meets that is exactly conserved in every known interaction. The unit also contains one of the cleanest pieces of evidence in all of physics: charge is quantised, and the quantum is exact.
facts: Charge is quantised: the elementary charge e = 1.602176634e-19 C exactly, and every observed charge in ordinary matter is an integer multiple of it.
Coulomb's law F = k q1 q2 / r^2 holds with k = 8.9875517923e9 N.m^2/C^2, and like charges repel while unlike charges attract.
Charge is conserved in every known interaction, and electric charge is an exact conserved quantum number in the Standard Model.
Charging by friction transfers electrons between surfaces; charging by induction moves electrons without any contact at all.
Conductors allow charge to move freely and insulators do not; in electrostatic equilibrium the field inside a conductor is zero and excess charge sits on the surface, concentrating at sharp points.
Earthing works because the Earth is an enormous conductor held at nearly constant potential.

Charge is quantised in units of e; the fractional charges seen in the fractional quantum Hall effect are a many-body property of a correlated electron liquid, not evidence that the electron is divisible.
conditions: Coulomb's law assumes static point charges in a uniform medium; extended bodies require integration and conductors require redistribution.
Charging by friction depends on the material pair, surface condition and humidity - the triboelectric order is a tendency, not a law.
The field inside a conductor is zero only in electrostatic equilibrium; a time-varying field drives currents inside it.
In semiconductors both electrons and holes carry current, so 'the charge carrier' model of a conductor has to be replaced by a two-carrier picture.
Coulomb's law is the static, vacuum result; for moving charges the magnetic field joins in, and an accelerating charge radiates, so the static formula alone no longer describes the system.

mysteries.question: Why is electric charge quantised, and can fractional charge ever be observed?
mysteries.note: The Standard Model contains charge quantisation but does not derive it; quasiparticles with fractional charge do exist in certain condensed-matter states, which is a different phenomenon.

mysteries.question: Is electric charge exactly conserved?

misconceptions.claim: Charging by friction creates charge, so a charged body has more charge than it had before.
misconceptions.why: Friction only separates and transfers electrons that were already there. The total charge of the system is conserved, and each body ends up with an equal and opposite charge.
misconceptions.correction: Rubbing transfers electrons from one surface to the other, so one body becomes negative and the other positive with equal magnitude. The total charge of the two-body system is unchanged; charge is conserved in every known interaction.

misconceptions.claim: Two identical conducting spheres in contact are given a charge Q. When they are separated, each carries Q/2.
misconceptions.why: That is true only if the spheres are identical and share the charge equally. If the spheres differ in size, the smaller one takes a larger share because its potential rises faster for the same charge, and the system has a unique equilibrium.
misconceptions.correction: For identical spheres, symmetry gives Q/2 each. For different spheres, the charge divides in proportion to their radii (for well-separated spheres), so the smaller sphere ends up with more than half the charge. The total is still Q.

misconceptions.claim: Coulomb's law applies to any two charged objects, whatever their shape and size.
misconceptions.why: The law is exact for point charges, or for spherically symmetric charge distributions. For extended bodies the force must be found by integration, and the result depends on the geometry.
misconceptions.correction: Coulomb's law F = k q1 q2 / r^2 holds for point charges in a uniform medium. For a uniformly charged spherical shell, the external field is exactly that of a point charge at the centre (the shell theorem) and the internal field is zero, so the law applies externally to spheres as well.

workbook.question: Two point charges of +2.0 microcoulomb and -3.0 microcoulomb are placed 0.50 m apart in air. Find the magnitude and direction of the force between them, and the force on a 1.0 microcoulomb charge placed on the line joining them, 0.20 m from the +2.0 microcoulomb charge.
workbook.answer: F = k q1 q2 / r^2 = 8.99 x 10^9 x (2.0 x 10^-6)(3.0 x 10^-6) / 0.25 = 8.99 x 10^9 x 6.0 x 10^-12 / 0.25 = 0.216 N, attractive because the charges have opposite signs. For the third charge, the field of the +2.0 microcoulomb charge at 0.20 m is E1 = k q1 / r^2 = 8.99 x 10^9 x 2.0 x 10^-6 / 0.04 = 4.5 x 10^5 N/C, directed away from the + charge (towards the -3.0 microcoulomb charge, 0.30 m away). The field of the -3.0 microcoulomb charge at that point is E2 = 8.99 x 10^9 x 3.0 x 10^-6 / 0.09 = 3.0 x 10^5 N/C, directed towards the - charge, i.e. in the same direction as E1. Net E = 7.5 x 10^5 N/C, so the force on the 1.0 microcoulomb charge is F = q E = 0.75 N in the same direction (towards the negative charge).

workbook.question: Use Gauss's law to show that the electric field outside a uniformly charged thin spherical shell of radius R and total charge Q is the same as that of a point charge Q at the centre, and that the field inside the shell is zero.
workbook.answer: Draw a concentric Gaussian sphere of radius r > R. By symmetry the field is radial and has the same magnitude everywhere on it, so the flux is E x 4 pi r^2. Gauss's law gives E x 4 pi r^2 = Q / epsilon0, so E = Q / (4 pi epsilon0 r^2) = k Q / r^2, exactly the field of a point charge at the centre. For r < R the same Gaussian surface encloses no charge, so the flux is zero; by symmetry E must be zero, and the field inside a charged shell is indeed zero. The same argument with a cylindrical Gaussian surface gives the field of an infinite line charge, E = lambda / (2 pi epsilon0 r), and with a pillbox gives the field of an infinite charged plane, E = sigma / (2 epsilon0).

workbook.question: Two identical metal spheres on insulating handles are in contact, and a charge Q is transferred onto the pair. They are then separated without discharging. Explain what happens to the charge on each sphere, and what would change if the spheres were of different sizes.
workbook.answer: While the spheres touch they behave as one conductor, and the charge Q spreads over the combined surface until the whole is at one potential. When they are separated, each keeps whatever charge it had at that moment, and the total remains Q. For identical spheres the symmetry of the situation means each carries Q/2. If the spheres have different radii, the smaller one has a smaller capacitance per unit charge and its potential rises more steeply, so at equilibrium the smaller sphere carries more than half of the charge; for well-separated spheres the split is in proportion to the radii, and the charge flows from the larger to the smaller sphere as they are brought apart, because the smaller sphere's potential is then higher. The physics is the same in both cases: charge flows until the two spheres are at the same potential.

units.summary: The electric field turns a force law into a description of the space around a charge: it says what force a test charge would feel at every point, whether or not one is actually there.
facts: The electric field is force per unit positive test charge, E = F/q, directed along the force on a positive test charge.
A point charge produces E = kq/r^2 directed radially, and superposition means the total field is the vector sum of the individual fields.
Field lines are a visualisation, not a count of anything: their density represents field strength, they start on positive charge and end on negative charge, and they never cross.
The field inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is zero; the field of an infinite non-conducting sheet is sigma/(2 epsilon0), and of a conducting sheet sigma/epsilon0.
Because F = qE for any charge, the field can be treated as an independent variable - the reason Gauss's law is so powerful.
A moving charge creates a magnetic field as well, so the electric and magnetic fields of a charge are two aspects of a single electromagnetic field.
Field lines are bookkeeping: the number crossing a surface is proportional to the flux, so a denser bundle means a stronger field, even though the lines themselves have no physical substance.
conditions: Closed-form field results exist only where symmetry is high enough - spherical, cylindrical or planar; any other distribution requires integration.
Electrostatic fields are conservative, so the work around a closed path vanishes and a scalar potential can be used instead.
In a dielectric the field is reduced by the relative permittivity, and polarisation P must be introduced; writing E = F/q with a 'free' charge only is wrong inside matter.
Electrostatic reasoning does not extend to time-varying fields: Maxwell's displacement current means a changing electric field generates a magnetic field.
Superposition is a statement about linear response, and real dielectrics are generally not linear, so polarisation and non-linear media need their own treatment.

mysteries.question: How does a charge act on matter that is not charged?
mysteries.note: The field picture handles it through polarisation; whether the field itself is physical or a bookkeeping device is a deeper interpretational question.

mysteries.question: Can a static field be completely screened in any geometry?
mysteries.note: Only conductors screen, and the shape of the screening conductor matters; a fully screened, shape-independent result is not generally available.

misconceptions.claim: Electric field lines are tubes of force carrying energy, so the number of lines meeting a surface tells you how much energy is there.
misconceptions.why: Field lines are a bookkeeping device, not physical threads. Their number is arbitrary and can be rescaled; what they represent is the direction of the field and, through their density, the strength of the field.
misconceptions.correction: A field line is drawn tangent to E at every point, and the number of lines crossing a surface is proportional to the flux through it, not to energy. The energy density of an electric field is (1/2) epsilon0 E^2, which depends on the field strength, not on any choice of line density.

misconceptions.claim: Inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium the electric field is zero, so a charged conductor has no field at all.
misconceptions.why: The field is zero only inside the material of the conductor. Outside the conductor the field is not zero, and for a charged conductor it extends into the surrounding space, falling off as 1/r^2 for a sphere.
misconceptions.correction: Free charges in a conductor move until the net force on them vanishes, so E = 0 within the material. The field outside the surface is perpendicular to it and is given by E = sigma / epsilon0 just outside, and by the equivalent point charge at the centre for a spherical conductor.

misconceptions.claim: An uncharged object is never affected by a charged one.
misconceptions.why: Charged objects polarise neutral ones: the charges in the neutral body redistribute, so it experiences a net attraction. This is why a charged rod picks up bits of paper.
misconceptions.correction: In a neutral conductor the free electrons move slightly towards or away from the charged rod, producing an induced dipole and a net attraction that survives even when the rod is subsequently removed. The effect is much weaker than the force between two charged objects, but it is real and it is how electrophoresis and electrostatic dust collection work.

workbook.question: Find the electric field at a point 10 cm from a point charge of 5.0 microcoulomb in air, and the force on an electron placed there.
workbook.answer: E = k q / r^2 = 8.99 x 10^9 x 5.0 x 10^-6 / (0.10)^2 = 8.99 x 10^9 x 5.0 x 10^-6 / 0.01 = 4.5 x 10^6 V/m, directed radially outward. The force on the electron is F = q E = 1.602 x 10^-19 x 4.5 x 10^6 = 7.2 x 10^-13 N, directed opposite to the field (inwards), because the electron is negatively charged.

workbook.question: Derive Gauss's law, integral form, from the fact that the flux of the field of a point charge through any closed surface is independent of the shape of that surface.
workbook.answer: For a point charge q, the field at distance r is E = q / (4 pi epsilon0 r^2). The flux through a closed surface S is the integral of E . dA; a spherical surface of radius r gives E x 4 pi r^2 = q / epsilon0. Because the field of a point charge is radial and its magnitude falls as 1/r^2, the same flux results for any closed surface enclosing the charge, and zero for a surface that does not. For a distribution of charges the total flux is the sum of the contributions, so the integral form is integral(S) E . dA = (1 / epsilon0) sum q_enclosed, or equivalently the differential form div E = rho / epsilon0. Superposition makes the result exact for any charge distribution, which is what makes Gauss's law the tool of choice for symmetric problems.

workbook.question: A charged glass rod is brought near, but not touching, a light metal sphere suspended on a thread. The sphere is attracted to the rod. Explain this, and predict what happens if the rod is touched to the sphere and then removed while the sphere is still close to the rod.
workbook.answer: The rod polarises the sphere: the free electrons in the metal shift slightly towards or away from the rod, so the near side of the sphere carries charge of opposite sign to the rod and the far side carries like charge. The nearer opposite charge is closer to the rod than the farther like charge, so the attraction outweighs the repulsion and the net force is towards the rod. On touching, charge flows between the rod and the sphere until they are at the same potential, and the sphere is left with a net charge of the same sign as the rod. When the rod is then removed, that net charge spreads uniformly over the sphere, and the force becomes repulsive. The attraction before contact is due to induction; the repulsion after contact is due to the transferred charge.

units.summary: Potential is the scalar alternative to the vector field. Because only differences are measurable, the zero of potential is a convention - and because the field is conservative, path never enters the answer.
facts: Electric potential is energy per unit charge, V = U/q, and a potential difference is the work done per unit charge by the field.
For a point charge V = kq/r with V tending to zero at infinity, and the potential difference is dV = -E.dl along any path.
Only potential differences are physically meaningful; the choice of zero is a convention, and it changes no experiment.
The potential energy of a system of point charges is the sum of pairwise terms q1 q2/(4 pi epsilon0 r_ij); the self-energy of a continuous distribution requires a self-consistent calculation.
Equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to field lines, and the work in moving a charge between two points on the same equipotential is zero.
Potential is a scalar, which is why circuit and field problems are often shorter in potential language than in field language.
Potential is defined only up to an additive constant, so only differences are physical; a conductor is one equipotential surface, and the field is minus the gradient of the potential.
conditions: The 1/r potential law assumes a point charge in vacuum; for a conductor the entire surface is one equipotential at a single value.
Potential differences are path-independent, so only the endpoints matter - but a potential difference between two points is not simply E.d unless the path is straight and along the field.
Moving a charge changes the stored energy of the whole system, and the work is shared between the field and the agent that moves it.
In a medium with permittivity epsilon the potential of a charge is reduced by the factor epsilon_r; the free charge does not change, the field does.
The expression U = qV holds for a conservative, time-independent field; in a time-varying field the work done on the charge also changes the energy stored in the field itself.

mysteries.question: How much energy is stored in an electromagnetic field, and how is it distributed in space?
mysteries.note: Classically the energy density is (1/2) epsilon E^2 plus a magnetic term; the quantum description in terms of photons remains less intuitive.

mysteries.question: Can energy be extracted usefully from the vacuum?
mysteries.note: Casimir and related effects are real and measurable but tiny; extracting macroscopic energy from vacuum fluctuations is not established.

misconceptions.claim: A charge at a point where the potential is zero must have zero potential energy.
misconceptions.why: Potential energy of a charge is q V, and the zero of potential is a matter of convention, not of physics. Moving the zero changes every potential energy by the same constant amount.
misconceptions.correction: Only differences in potential are physical. A charge can have a large potential energy in one convention and a small one in another, and the force it feels depends only on the gradient of the potential, never on the value at a point.

misconceptions.claim: A negative potential means a negative potential energy and therefore a force pushing the charge the wrong way.
misconceptions.why: The sign of the potential energy depends on the sign of the charge as well as on the potential, and the force is set by the field, which points from high to low potential.
misconceptions.correction: For a negative charge, U = q V is positive where V is negative, and the force on it is F = q E, which points towards higher potential. The rule to remember is: a positive charge moves towards lower potential, a negative charge towards higher potential.

misconceptions.claim: Because potential is a scalar, the work done to bring a charge in from infinity is independent of the path taken.
misconceptions.why: That is right, and the reason is that the electrostatic field is conservative - the work depends only on the endpoints. But the path independence comes from the field, not from the potential being a scalar.
misconceptions.correction: The field of a charge distribution is conservative, so the line integral of E . dl depends only on the end points and equals -(V_final - V_initial). Scalars alone would not guarantee this: the magnetic field is also expressible with a scalar potential in some situations, yet the work done by it around a closed loop is generally not zero.

workbook.question: Find the potential at a point 30 cm from a point charge of +2.0 microcoulomb in air, and the potential energy of an electron at that point.
workbook.answer: V = k q / r = 8.99 x 10^9 x 2.0 x 10^-6 / 0.30 = 5.99 x 10^4 V (about 60 kV). The potential energy of the electron is U = q V = (-1.602 x 10^-19)(5.99 x 10^4) = -9.6 x 10^-15 J, which is -60 eV, since an electron volt is 1.602 x 10^-19 J. The negative sign reflects attraction to the positive source charge.

workbook.question: Derive the potential at a point a distance r from a point charge Q, and then the potential energy of a second charge q placed there.
workbook.answer: The potential difference is defined by V_B - V_A = -integral(A to B) E . dl. For a point charge the field is radial, E = k Q / r^2, so moving from a point at infinity to a point at distance r gives V(r) - V(infinity) = -integral(infinity to r) k Q / r'^2 dr' = + k Q / r. With V(infinity) = 0, V = k Q / r, and more generally V(r) = k Q / r + constant. The potential energy of a charge q at that point is U = q V = k q Q / r, since the definition of the potential energy of a charge in a field is U = q V. Note that only differences in V, and hence only differences in U, are physically meaningful.

workbook.question: A proton is released from rest in the field of a fixed negative charge. Describe the motion in terms of potential and potential energy, and say what quantity is conserved, and why the proton's speed increases even though its potential energy decreases.
workbook.answer: The proton starts at some potential V and potential energy U = e V, and the field accelerates it towards the negative charge, i.e. towards higher potential. As it moves, its potential energy decreases and its kinetic energy increases by exactly the same amount, because the field is conservative and the work done by it is the negative of the change in potential energy. The total energy U + K is therefore conserved; no energy is created, it is converted from potential to kinetic form. The proton's speed is greatest near the source charge, where the potential energy is most negative, and would become infinite only if it were allowed to spiral into the source - in practice it radiates and the classical picture breaks down.

units.summary: A capacitor is an energy store defined by geometry and dielectric. The unit is where the parallel-plate formula gets derived from Gauss's law, and where students first meet the gap between an ideal component and a real one.
facts: Capacitance is C = Q/V; for a parallel-plate capacitor C = epsilon0 epsilon_r A/d, so capacitance grows with area and shrinks with separation.
The energy stored is U = (1/2) C V^2 = Q^2/(2C), and the energy density in the dielectric is u = (1/2) epsilon E^2.
Capacitors in parallel add capacitance; in series the reciprocals add.
A capacitor stores energy rather than supplying it: an ideal charged capacitor discharges through any available path, and the discharge time constant is R C.
Real capacitors are limited by dielectric breakdown, leakage current, equivalent series resistance and self-inductance at high frequency.
Supercapacitors deliver far more power than batteries but store far less energy per kilogram, and the two technologies occupy different niches for that reason.

Capacitance depends on geometry and dielectric only, never on the charge or the voltage: adding dielectric raises the capacitance by the permittivity ratio, and a connected battery supplies the extra charge at unchanged voltage.
conditions: The parallel-plate formula assumes the separation is much smaller than the plate dimensions, so fringing can be ignored, and that the dielectric fills the gap uniformly.
In a dielectric the bound charges reduce the field by 1/epsilon_r, but the energy per unit volume usually still increases because polarisation contributes.
At DC, leakage limits how long a charge can be held; at high frequency, inductance and ESR dominate, and the ideal capacitor stops being a capacitor.
Electrolytic capacitors are polar and will be destroyed by reverse voltage, while ceramic and film types are non-polar but have different leakage and stability behaviour.
The stored energy lives in the electric field, not in the charges; discharging a capacitor does not lose that energy, it converts it back into current and heat.

mysteries.question: How can more energy be stored at a higher voltage in a smaller volume?
mysteries.note: Solid electrolytes, nanostructured dielectrics and breakdown engineering are all being pursued, and each trades cost, reliability and lifetime against energy density.

mysteries.question: Is there a fundamental upper bound to the energy that can be stored in a given volume?
mysteries.note: Fundamental limits exist, including the scale at which the vacuum itself breaks down, but they lie far above present engineering practice.

misconceptions.claim: A capacitor stores charge, and the energy of a charged capacitor is the energy of the charges it holds.
misconceptions.why: The energy is stored in the electric field between the plates, not in the charges themselves. A charged capacitor that is short-circuited loses all its energy in the spark, even though the charge on the plates was never 'used up'.
misconceptions.correction: The stored energy is U = (1/2) C V^2 = Q^2 / (2C) = (1/2) Q V, and it is the energy of the field. Equivalently the energy density is (1/2) epsilon0 E^2, so energy is stored wherever the field is - between the plates, not on them.

misconceptions.claim: Capacitors in series add their capacitances, exactly as resistors in series add their resistances.
misconceptions.why: In series the same charge is on every capacitor, and the total voltage is the sum of the voltage drops; since V = Q/C, the reciprocal rule follows. In parallel the voltages are equal and the charges add, so the capacitances add directly.
misconceptions.correction: Parallel: C = C1 + C2 + ...; series: 1/C = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + ..., so the series combination is always smaller than the smallest capacitor. This is the opposite of the resistor rule, and the standard exam trap.

misconceptions.claim: The capacitance of a capacitor depends on the charge stored on it.
misconceptions.why: Capacitance is fixed by the geometry and by the dielectric; it is the property that makes V proportional to Q. If C depended on Q, the relation V = Q/C would not be linear.
misconceptions.correction: C = epsilon0 epsilon_r A / d for a parallel-plate capacitor depends only on the plate area, the separation and the dielectric. The charge and voltage change with the situation; C does not.

workbook.question: A 10 microfarad capacitor is charged to 12 V and then disconnected from the battery. Find the charge stored and the energy in the capacitor, and the energy per unit volume if the plates are 5 cm square and separated by 2 mm.
workbook.answer: Q = C V = 10 x 10^-6 x 12 = 1.2 x 10^-4 C (120 microcoulomb). Energy U = (1/2) C V^2 = 0.5 x 10 x 10^-6 x 144 = 7.2 x 10^-4 J. The plate area is A = (0.05)^2 = 2.5 x 10^-3 m^2 and the volume of field is A d = 2.5 x 10^-3 x 2 x 10^-3 = 5 x 10^-6 m^3, so the energy density is 7.2 x 10^-4 / 5 x 10^-6 = 144 J/m^3. (After disconnection the charge and the energy are unchanged.)

workbook.question: Derive the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor and the energy it stores, using Gauss's law for the field between the plates.
workbook.answer: Between large parallel plates of area A carrying charges of density sigma = Q/A, a Gaussian pillbox straddling one plate gives E A = sigma A / epsilon0, so E = sigma / epsilon0 = Q / (epsilon0 A). The potential difference between the plates separated by d is V = E d = Q d / (epsilon0 A). Hence C = Q / V = epsilon0 A / d, and with a dielectric of relative permittivity epsilon_r, C = epsilon0 epsilon_r A / d. The energy stored is obtained from the work done in charging: U = integral from 0 to Q of (q/C) dq = Q^2 / (2C) = (1/2) C V^2. The field is uniform only away from the edges, so the derivation assumes the plate separation is small compared with the plate dimensions.

workbook.question: A 2 microfarad and a 3 microfarad capacitor are connected in series across a 12 V battery, and then, while still connected, a third capacitor is added in parallel with the 2 microfarad one. Find the charges and voltages across the capacitors before and after the change.
workbook.answer: Initially, in series, the same charge is on both: 1/C = 1/2 + 1/3, so C = 1.2 microfarad and Q = C V = 1.2 x 12 = 14.4 microcoulomb on each. The 2 microfarad capacitor has 7.2 V across it and the 3 microfarad one 4.8 V. Adding a 3 microfarad capacitor in parallel with the 2 microfarad one makes a 5 microfarad combination; in series with 3 microfarad the total is 1/(1/5 + 1/3) = 1.875 microfarad, so the charge on the series string becomes 1.875 x 12 = 22.5 microcoulomb. The 5 microfarad pair carries 22.5 microcoulomb at 4.5 V and the 3 microfarad one carries 22.5 microcoulomb at 7.5 V. The lesson is the practical one: a small capacitor in series with a large one takes a disproportionate share of the voltage, and connecting a battery across an isolated small capacitor can exceed its rating.

units.summary: Circuit analysis is conservation law with a convenient vocabulary: charge conservation becomes Kirchhoff's current law, energy conservation becomes the loop law, and Ohm's law is the constitutive relation that connects them - where it is allowed to apply.
facts: Ohm's law V = IR describes ohmic components only; a filament lamp and a diode are non-ohmic, with resistance that changes as current or temperature changes.
Kirchhoff's current law is charge conservation at a node; the loop law is energy conservation around a closed path.
Series resistances add and parallel conductances add, so series-parallel reduction is the workhorse method for solvable networks.
A source with internal resistance r delivers V = E - Ir, so its terminal voltage falls as the current it supplies rises.
Maximum power transfer to the load occurs when the load resistance equals the internal resistance, but then only half of the generated power reaches the load.
Joule heating P = I^2 R is why conductors and components get hot, and rated wattage is what limits safe operation.
Kirchhoff's laws are bookkeeping identities - charge conservation and energy conservation in disguise - so they hold for any lumped circuit regardless of the physics of the individual elements.
conditions: The lumped-circuit model assumes ideal wires and components that are small compared with the wavelength; at high frequencies transmission lines and distributed effects take over.
Kirchhoff's laws assume quasi-static behaviour, so no charge accumulates inside the wires and each node has a well-defined potential.
Ohmic behaviour is temperature-dependent, so treating R as constant is an approximation that matters in power calculations.
A real battery is not a fixed source: its terminal voltage and internal resistance both depend on state of charge, temperature and current.
Series and parallel reduction assumes ideal wires and lumped elements; at high frequency the wire's own resistance and inductance take over and the ideal rules stop holding.

mysteries.question: What sets the energy floor for computing with superconducting circuits?
mysteries.note: Superconducting qubits and single-photon detectors push towards the energy-time uncertainty limit for readout, which is now the binding constraint in several architectures.

mysteries.question: Can computation be performed with less energy per operation than a transistor switch requires?
mysteries.note: Landauer sets a thermodynamic floor and the end of Moore's-law scaling has moved the constraint into interconnect and memory energy.

misconceptions.claim: Ohm's law V = IR applies to every component, so every resistor has a fixed resistance.
misconceptions.why: Ohm's law is a statement about a class of materials whose resistance does not change with the applied voltage. Many everyday components are not ohmic.
misconceptions.correction: For a metal conductor at constant temperature, R is constant and V is proportional to I. A filament lamp is non-ohmic: as the current rises the filament heats, its resistance rises and the V-I graph curves. A diode is strongly non-ohmic and conducts in only one direction.

misconceptions.claim: The current in a circuit is consumed by the components it passes through.
misconceptions.why: Current is the rate of flow of charge and is conserved everywhere in a series circuit; energy is transferred, not charge.
misconceptions.correction: Charge is conserved: the same charge per second passes through every element of a series circuit, which is Kirchhoff's current law. What is 'used up' is energy: the potential energy of the charges falls as they do work against resistance, and that energy becomes heat.

misconceptions.claim: A voltmeter connected in series across a component measures the drop across it.
misconceptions.why: A voltmeter must be connected in parallel, and an ammeter in series. A voltmeter in series has a very large resistance, so it effectively opens the circuit.
misconceptions.correction: Voltmeters have a very high resistance (ideally infinite) and are connected in parallel with the component; ammeters have a very low resistance and are connected in series. Connecting a voltmeter in series leaves almost no current, and the reading is then the supply voltage rather than a drop across the component.

workbook.question: A cell of emf 12 V and internal resistance 0.50 ohm is connected to a load of 5.5 ohm. Find the current, the terminal voltage of the cell and the power delivered to the load.
workbook.answer: I = E / (R + r) = 12 / (5.5 + 0.5) = 2.0 A. Terminal voltage V = E - I r = 12 - 2.0 x 0.5 = 11 V (and V = I R = 2.0 x 5.5 = 11 V, as it must be). Power in the load P = I V = 2.0 x 11 = 22 W. The power lost inside the cell is I^2 r = 4.0 x 0.5 = 2.0 W, and the total power supplied by the cell is E I = 24 W, so the energy balance is 22 + 2 = 24 W.

workbook.question: Derive Kirchhoff's loop law from the conservation of energy, and show that the sum of the potential changes around any closed loop in a circuit is zero.
workbook.answer: Take any closed loop in a steady circuit. Around the loop, the work done by the electric field in moving a charge q once around must be zero, because the charge returns to its starting point with the same energy: the electrostatic field is conservative, so the work around a closed path vanishes. The work done by the field in moving the charge through each element is q times the potential change across it, so q sum(delta V) = 0 and sum(delta V) = 0. In terms of the circuit elements, the sum of the emf contributions equals the sum of the voltage drops: sum(E) = sum(I R). The same argument applied to a node, where charge is neither created nor destroyed, gives Kirchhoff's current law, sum(I_in) = sum(I_out).

workbook.question: Explain, using the V-I characteristic of a filament lamp, why a lamp of rated 100 W, 230 V behaves differently from a resistor when the supply voltage is varied, and what happens if the supply voltage is suddenly increased.
workbook.answer: For a metal resistor the resistance is constant, so I is proportional to V and the power rises as V^2. For a filament lamp the current heats the filament, the metal becomes hotter, its resistance rises (the resistivity of a metal increases with temperature), and the V-I curve bends upwards, so the current grows less than proportionally. The rated values 100 W and 230 V give a nominal current of 0.435 A and a resistance of 529 ohms at the working temperature, but the cold resistance is much smaller, which is why a lamp struck from cold draws a large initial current and the filament glows up over a fraction of a second. If the supply voltage is raised, the operating point moves up the curve, the filament runs hotter, its resistance is still higher, and the power - and the temperature, and the rate of evaporation of the filament - rise sharply, which is why overvoltage shortens the life of a lamp.

units.summary: Nuclear physics is where conservation laws become non-negotiable and where a handful of nucleons produce an enormous energy scale. The binding-energy curve is the centre of the unit: it explains why fusion and fission both release energy, and only in different regimes.
facts: The nuclear radius scales as R = R0 A^(1/3) with R0 about 1.2 fm, which means nuclear density is roughly constant at about 2.3e17 kg/m^3.
Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56 at about 8.8 MeV per nucleon, so fusion up to iron and fission beyond it both release energy.
Einstein's E = mc^2 converts the mass defect into binding energy; 1 u of mass corresponds to 931.5 MeV.
Radioactive decay is statistical: the half-life is a property of the nucleus, and no individual atom decides when it decays.
Neutron decay and nuclear reactions conserve charge, baryon number, energy, momentum and angular momentum, and every proposed reaction must satisfy all of them.
Doubly magic nuclei such as oxygen-16, with closed proton and neutron shells, show binding energies well above the smooth trend of their neighbours.
Binding energy per nucleon climbs to iron-56 and falls beyond it, which is the whole reason fusion powers stars and fission powers reactors: both release energy by moving matter towards the peak.
conditions: The semi-empirical mass formula is fitted to known nuclei, so its predictions are most reliable in the region where the coefficients were fitted and degrade for exotic nuclei.
Alpha decay proceeds by quantum tunnelling, and the extreme sensitivity of the half-life to the alpha energy and Q-value - the Geiger-Nuttall relation - is the essential experimental handle.
Fission and fusion release energy only because the products sit nearer the peak of the binding-energy curve than the fuel does.
Quasi-stable nuclei are predicted by the liquid-drop model, but shell effects require the nuclear shell model, and neither is exact.
The liquid-drop model gets nuclear masses roughly right but misses the shell and pairing effects that explain the magic numbers and the fine structure of fission barriers.

mysteries.note: Magic numbers are firmly established experimentally, but their quantitative origin in the nucleon-nucleon interaction remains a subtle many-body problem.

mysteries.note: The neutron is not a point particle, and its charge and magnetic structure is being probed at accelerators and in precision atomic-physics experiments.
