misconceptions.claim: A heavier nucleus is always more tightly bound, so the most massive nuclei are the most stable.
misconceptions.why: Binding energy per nucleon is not monotonic in mass number. It rises to a maximum near iron-56 and then falls, which is why heavy nuclei are unstable and can release energy by fission.
misconceptions.correction: The binding energy per nucleon is about 8.8 MeV at iron-56, about 7.6 MeV for uranium-238 and about 1.1 MeV for a lead nucleus at the extreme end. Nuclei heavier than iron gain energy by splitting, and nuclei lighter than iron gain it by fusing, because in both cases the products lie closer to the maximum of the curve.

misconceptions.claim: A radioactive atom decays because it is unstable and 'spits out' radiation at a random moment.
misconceptions.why: The decay is not a random event in the sense of being unpredictable in principle: the probability per unit time is fixed by the nucleus, but the instant at which any particular nucleus decays is not determined in advance.
misconceptions.correction: Radioactive decay obeys the law dN/dt = -lambda N, with a half-life T = ln2 / lambda that is a property of the isotope, not of the individual atom. Over many nuclei the law is exact; for a single nucleus only the probability is known. This statistical character is the basis of radiometric dating.

misconceptions.claim: In nuclear reactions mass is not conserved, because mass can be converted into energy.
misconceptions.why: Mass is not lost; it is the total mass-energy that is conserved. The 'missing' mass in a reaction is exactly the mass equivalent of the released energy, and the rest masses of the products add to more than the rest mass of the reactants.
misconceptions.correction: In every reaction the total mass-energy, and therefore the total baryon number and the total charge, is conserved. For example, 4 neutrons converting into a helium nucleus release 0.006 u of mass, which is 5.6 MeV of energy, and the sum of the rest masses of the products is greater than the sum of the rest masses of the reactants by exactly that amount.

workbook.question: Find the energy equivalent of 1 unified atomic mass unit, and the energy released in the fusion of four protons to form one helium-4 nucleus with the release of two positrons and two neutrinos (mass defect about 0.0187 u).
workbook.answer: 1 u = 1.66054 x 10^-27 kg, so E = m c^2 = 1.66054 x 10^-27 x (2.9979 x 10^8)^2 = 1.4924 x 10^-10 J. In electron volts, 1.4924 x 10^-10 / 1.602 x 10^-19 = 9.315 x 10^8 eV = 931.5 MeV. For the fusion reaction, the mass defect of 0.0187 u corresponds to 0.0187 x 931.5 = 17.4 MeV, which is the energy released per helium-4 nucleus produced. This is the basis of fusion in the Sun and in thermonuclear weapons.

workbook.question: Derive the binding energy per nucleon of a nucleus from the masses of its constituent nucleons, and explain why the packing fraction is the useful measure of the energy released.
workbook.answer: The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of the masses of its free nucleons by the mass defect, dm = Z m_p + (A - Z) m_n - m_nucleus. The missing mass is the mass of the energy that holds the nucleus together, so the binding energy is B = dm c^2, and the binding energy per nucleon is B / A. The packing fraction is f = dm / (Z m_p + (A - Z) m_n), the fraction of the mass that is converted into binding energy, so B = f A (sum of the free nucleon masses) c^2. For iron-56, f is about 0.0087 and B/A is about 8.8 MeV per nucleon, the maximum of the curve; for uranium-238, f is about 0.0071 and B/A about 7.6 MeV.

workbook.question: Explain, using the binding energy per nucleon curve, why both fission of a heavy nucleus and fusion of a light nucleus release energy, while the splitting of a mid-mass nucleus absorbs energy.
workbook.answer: The binding energy per nucleon is a measure of how tightly bound each nucleon is, and a reaction releases energy when the products have a greater total binding energy than the reactants. For uranium-238, B/A is about 7.6 MeV; the fission products around mass 95 have B/A of about 8.5 MeV, so the products are more tightly bound and the difference, about 200 MeV, is released. For four protons, B/A is effectively zero since free protons are not bound, while the helium-4 product has B/A of 28.3/4 = 7.1 MeV, so about 28 MeV is released. Near the maximum of the curve, at iron-56, splitting a nucleus moves the products to a lower B/A, so the process absorbs energy instead. This single curve explains why the iron group is the end point of stellar fusion and why both fission and fusion are viable energy sources.

units.summary: Solid-state physics explains why metals conduct and insulators do not, why semiconductors conduct better when heated and metals worse, and why resistance can vanish altogether below a critical temperature.
facts: In a solid, allowed energy levels broaden into bands; overlapping bands make a metal, while a gap between the valence and conduction bands makes a semiconductor or an insulator.
In a metal the conductivity falls as temperature rises because more scattering; in a semiconductor it rises because more carriers are excited across the gap.
The Fermi level sits at the top of the occupied states at 0 K in a metal, and the Fermi energy of copper is about 7 eV.
Carrier concentration in a semiconductor follows n proportional to T^(3/2) exp(-Eg/2kT), so the temperature dependence is exponential and steep.
Doping shifts the Fermi level and produces n-type or p-type material; the band gap itself is unchanged by doping.
Below the critical temperature a superconductor has exactly zero resistance and expels magnetic fields (the Meissner effect); BCS theory explains conventional superconductors through Cooper pairs.
The band structure is one object that explains whether a solid conducts, whether it is a semiconductor, and whether it becomes superconducting when it gets cold.
conditions: Band theory assumes a periodic potential, so it describes crystals well and amorphous or strongly disordered materials poorly.
BCS theory accounts for conventional phonon-mediated superconductors but not the high-temperature cuprates, for which a complete microscopic understanding is still outstanding.
Superconductivity requires all three of T below T_c, current density below the critical value, and field below the critical field.
The temperature dependence of a semiconductor is exponential only in the extrinsic or intrinsic regimes described by the model; heavy doping and high fields break that description.
The nearly-free-electron model treats the ions as a periodic potential and the electrons as free particles; it breaks down for narrow bands, strong correlations and the high-temperature cuprates.

mysteries.question: What is the microscopic mechanism of high-temperature superconductivity in cuprates?
mysteries.note: The US Department of Energy notes that a complete understanding of these newer materials remains an outstanding problem.

mysteries.question: Can the critical temperature of a superconductor be predicted from its structure and composition?
mysteries.note: Deliberately doping a material has raised its critical temperature, and ORNL reports advances in hunting better superconducting materials, but reliable prediction remains out of reach.

syllabusTopics: Difference between metals, insulators and semiconductors using band theory

misconceptions.claim: An insulator has no electrons, while a metal has free electrons that move freely through the lattice.
misconceptions.why: Every solid has electrons. The difference is the band structure: in a metal the valence band and the conduction band overlap, whereas in an insulator a band gap separates a full valence band from an empty conduction band.
misconceptions.correction: An insulator has as many electrons as a metal; they are simply bound in a full valence band, and the energy needed to reach the conduction band (the band gap) is far too large for thermal energy at ordinary temperatures. A semiconductor has a small gap (about 1.12 eV for silicon), so some electrons are thermally excited across it, which is why its conductivity rises with temperature.

misconceptions.claim: Doping adds free charge carriers to a semiconductor.
misconceptions.why: Doping does not add carriers directly; it adds impurity levels close to the band edges, and the carriers appear when those levels are ionised, by thermal energy in n-type material or by the release of bound electrons in p-type.
misconceptions.correction: In n-type silicon, a group V donor (for example phosphorus) contributes a fifth valence electron which is only weakly bound and is easily promoted into the conduction band, leaving a fixed positive ion behind. In p-type material, a group III acceptor (for example boron) has one fewer valence electron, so an electron is drawn from the valence band, leaving a mobile hole. The Fermi level shifts into the conduction band for n-type and into the valence band for p-type.

misconceptions.claim: The Fermi level is the highest energy level occupied by electrons in the metal.
misconceptions.why: That is true only at 0 K. At any temperature above absolute zero, states above the Fermi level are occupied with a probability given by the Fermi-Dirac distribution, and the occupancy at the Fermi level itself is one half.
misconceptions.correction: At T = 0 K the Fermi level is the highest occupied state. At finite T, f(E) = 1/(exp((E - E_F)/kT) + 1), so f(E_F) = 1/2 and the occupancy falls away over an energy range of a few kT around E_F. For copper, E_F is about 7 eV while kT at room temperature is only about 0.026 eV, which is why the everyday description of a metal as a filled band with a sharp edge is a good approximation, whereas for a semiconductor with a 1.12 eV gap the same approximation fails completely.

workbook.question: Silicon has a band gap of 1.12 eV. Find the wavelength of the longest-wavelength photon that can excite a valence electron across the gap, and state whether visible light can do this.
workbook.answer: The threshold photon energy is E = 1.12 eV. Using E = hc/lambda with hc = 1240 eV nm, lambda = 1240 / 1.12 = 1107 nm = 1.11 x 10^-6 m, in the near infrared. Visible light (about 380 to 750 nm) has photon energies of 3.3 to 1.65 eV, all above the 1.12 eV gap, so visible photons can excite electrons across the silicon gap - which is exactly why silicon solar cells respond to visible light and not to the infrared beyond 1.11 microns.

workbook.question: Derive the temperature dependence of the intrinsic carrier concentration in a semiconductor, n = n_i = sqrt(N_C N_V) exp(-E_g / 2 k T), and explain the opposite trends for a metal and a semiconductor.
workbook.answer: In an intrinsic semiconductor the number of thermally excited electrons equals the number of holes, n = p = n_i, and the mass action law np = n_i^2 holds. The effective densities of states in the conduction and valence bands are N_C = 2(2 pi m_e k T / h^2)^(3/2) and N_V = 2(2 pi m_h k T / h^2)^(3/2), each proportional to T^(3/2). The probability of an electron occupying a state just above the conduction band edge is exp(-E_g / 2 kT) by Boltzmann statistics, so n = sqrt(N_C N_V) exp(-E_g / 2 kT), which is proportional to T^(3/2) exp(-E_g / 2kT). The exponential factor dominates for a small band gap, so n rises steeply with temperature. In a metal the relevant electrons are already in the conduction band, and the effect of heating is to increase the lattice vibrations, so the mean free path and the conductivity fall. Hence the resistance of a metal rises with temperature while that of a semiconductor falls.

workbook.question: A superconductor has exactly zero resistance below a critical temperature. Explain what the Meissner effect adds to this statement, and why zero resistance alone is not enough to identify a superconductor.
workbook.answer: Zero resistance says only that a current, once established, persists without decay. The Meissner effect says that when a material is cooled below its critical temperature it expels magnetic flux from its interior, so the field inside becomes zero except in a penetration depth of about 100 nm at the surface. This is a distinct thermodynamic property: a perfect conductor with zero resistance that was cooled in a field would keep that field trapped, while a superconductor expels it. Zero resistance is also not unique: a perfect conductor cooled in a field behaves the same way, and a low-resistance material such as copper at liquid-helium temperature has a resistance far below any measurement. Superconductivity is therefore identified by the combination of zero resistance and flux expulsion below a critical temperature, together with the critical field, the critical current and the critical temperature as separate limits.

units.summary: The final unit is about the edge of the subject: the Standard Model and where it stops, the detection of gravitational waves and neutrino oscillations, and the questions that a generation of experiments is now narrowing - slowly, and honestly.
facts: The Standard Model describes the particles and forces that have been confirmed in the laboratory, but it does not explain dark matter, dark energy, quantum gravity, or the cosmic matter-antimatter imbalance.

The LHCb collaboration at CERN observed CP violation in baryon decays - announced in March 2025 and published in Nature in July 2025 - adding a piece to the matter-antimatter puzzle, though the Standard Model's CP violation remains far too small to explain the observed imbalance (CERN).
The Higgs field gives mass to the W and Z bosons and to fermions through the Yukawa coupling, and the Higgs boson was observed at the LHC in 2012.
Neutrino oscillation proved that neutrinos have mass, which reshaped how the Standard Model is interpreted.
Gravitational waves were first detected in 2015 by LIGO, opening a new observational window on the universe.
Experiments in the frontier are statements of probability with controlled systematics: evidence means a statistically significant deviation, not proof.
The Standard Model accounts for three of the four forces and every confirmed particle, but not dark matter, dark energy, quantum gravity, or the matter-antimatter asymmetry.
conditions: Every frontier claim carries an uncertainty; a null result constrains the strength of a coupling rather than proving absence.
The Standard Model is an effective description validated at the energies tested, and new physics could appear above them without invalidating it.
Numerical simulation is a third pillar of the subject, and it must be validated against analytically solvable limits and against experiment.
Observational limits and theoretical predictions live on different timescales; a bound announced by an experiment can tighten long before a theory explains it.
The Higgs field gives mass to the W and Z bosons and to the fermions, but most of the mass of everyday matter comes from the binding energy inside protons and neutrons, not from the Higgs.

mysteries.question: Why is there far more matter than antimatter in the universe?
mysteries.note: CP violation is necessary but, in the Standard Model, far too small; mechanisms such as leptogenesis are candidate explanations under active study (CERN).

mysteries.question: What drives the accelerating expansion of the universe?
mysteries.note: The observations are secure; the mechanism is not, and no confirmed detection of the responsible particle has been made.

mysteries.question: Does gravity admit a consistent quantum description?
mysteries.note: No fully consistent theory exists, and the attempts to build one have not yet produced testable predictions.

misconceptions.claim: The Standard Model explains all four fundamental forces.
misconceptions.why: It describes the electromagnetic, the strong and the weak interactions with remarkable precision, but gravity is not included, and the neutrino masses and the cosmological constant are not accommodated by the minimal model.
misconceptions.correction: The Standard Model is a quantum field theory of the electromagnetic, weak and strong interactions; gravity is described separately by general relativity, and no verified quantum theory that includes gravity exists. Its predictions have been tested to extraordinary precision, and no confirmed deviation from it has been found, but it is not a theory of everything.

misconceptions.claim: Antiparticles are exotic heavy partners created only in high-energy laboratories.
misconceptions.why: The electron's antiparticle, the positron, is the same mass and is found in ordinary cosmic rays and in medical imaging. Every particle of matter has an antiparticle of the same mass.
misconceptions.correction: For each particle there is an antiparticle of equal mass and opposite charge, lepton number and, for baryons, baryon number. The electron and positron annihilate into photons; quarks and antiquarks do the same, and mesons are themselves quark-antiquark pairs.

misconceptions.claim: Because neutrinos were once thought to be massless, their detection in 2015 settled the question of their mass.
misconceptions.why: Neutrino oscillation experiments showed that the flavours change along the flight, which requires the mass eigenstates to differ in mass, but the oscillation pattern measures differences of squared masses, not the masses themselves.
misconceptions.correction: Oscillation experiments constrain the differences delta m^2, and the absolute scale is set by other data, principally the shape of the solar neutrino spectrum and the endpoint of electron-neutrino beta decay, as in KATRIN. The current bound is a neutrino mass below about 0.45 eV/c^2, and the ordering of the masses is still an open question.

workbook.question: Find the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through a potential difference of 100 V, and compare it with the wavelength of the same electron in its ground state in an atom.
workbook.answer: The kinetic energy gained is e V = 100 eV = 1.602 x 10^-17 J, so the momentum is p = sqrt(2 m E) = sqrt(2 x 9.109 x 10^-31 x 1.602 x 10^-17) = sqrt(2.918 x 10^-47) = 5.40 x 10^-24 kg m/s, and the wavelength is lambda = h / p = 6.626 x 10^-34 / 5.40 x 10^-24 = 1.23 x 10^-10 m = 0.123 nm. This is comparable with atomic spacings, which is why the electron shows wave behaviour in the electron microscope. By contrast, the wavelength of an electron bound in an atom with an energy of a few electron volts is of the order of 0.1 to 0.3 nm, and for a nucleus of a few MeV it is of the order of 10^-15 m.

workbook.question: Derive the photoelectric equation from Planck's hypothesis and Einstein's photon model, and state the threshold frequency.
workbook.answer: Planck's hypothesis says that a blackbody radiates in quanta of energy E = h nu. Einstein proposed that light itself consists of photons of this energy. In the photoelectric effect an electron absorbs one photon, of energy h nu; part of this goes into the work required to escape from the metal, W = h nu_0, the work function, and the remainder becomes kinetic energy. Conservation of energy therefore gives h nu = W + (1/2) m v_max^2, which is the photoelectric equation. The threshold frequency is the frequency at which the electron just escapes with zero kinetic energy, nu_0 = W / h, so no emission occurs below it however intense the radiation. The equation also explains why the maximum kinetic energy depends on the frequency and not on the intensity, which is the classical prediction the wave theory cannot make.

workbook.question: Neutrino oscillation was discovered when the measured flux of electron neutrinos from the Sun was about one third of the expected value. Explain how this observation leads to the conclusion that neutrinos have mass, and what the observation does not tell you.
workbook.answer: The deficit cannot be explained by loss of flux: the neutral-current measurements show that the total number of neutrinos arriving is essentially the expected one, so the electron neutrinos have changed into other flavours (muon and tau neutrinos), a process called oscillation. Oscillation requires the three neutrino mass eigenstates to have different masses, because the flavour states are superpositions of the mass eigenstates and the phases of the components evolve at different rates, so the probability of finding a given flavour depends on the distance travelled and on the differences of the squared masses. What the observation does not give is the absolute mass: the oscillation probability depends only on delta m^2, so any set of masses with the same differences fits the data equally well, and the absolute scale has to be fixed by other measurements. A further puzzle is the flavour ratio itself, which for the standard solar model should be about 1:2:0, but is measured as about 1:1:1.
